country.title: Romania
country.text:
Romania is a country in Central and Southeastern Europe. It lies on the lower course of the Danube, north of the Balkan Peninsula, and on the northwestern shore of the Black Sea. It borders Ukraine to the north and east, Hungary to the west, Serbia to the southwest, Bulgaria to the south, Moldova to the east, and the Black Sea to the southeast. It is the twelfth-largest country in Europe by area, covering 238,397 km2 (92,046 mi2), and the sixth-most populous member state of the European Union, with 19 million inhabitants. The capital, largest city and economic centre is Bucharest. Other major cities include Cluj-Napoca, Iași, Constanța, Timișoara, Brașov and Craiova.
Romania was settled during the Lower Paleolithic. In antiquity its territory was inhabited by the Dacians. Part of it became the Roman province of Dacia after Trajan's Dacian Wars, beginning the process of Romanisation. The modern Romanian state was formed in 1859 through the unification of Moldavia and Wallachia under Alexandru Ioan Cuza, and adopted the name Romania in 1866. Romania gained independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1877, which was recognised by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878, and became the Kingdom of Romania in 1881 under Carol I. As a result of its participation in the Second Balkan War, Romania acquired Southern Dobruja from Bulgaria in 1913, concluded by the Treaty of Bucharest.
During World War I, Romania joined the Allies in 1916. The Great Union was a series of political unions proclaimed in 1918. After World War I, most of the claimed territories from Kingdom of Hungary (Banat, Crișana, Maramureș, Transylvania) were granted to Kingdom of Romania under the Treaty of Trianon in 1920. The union with Bukovina was recognized in 1919 by the Treaty of Saint-Germain and the union with Bessarabia was recognized in 1920 by the Treaty of Paris. Greater Romania was formed, which reached its largest territorial extent. In 1938, King Carol II suspended the constitution and established a royal dictatorship. In 1940, Romania lost Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina to the Soviet Union, Northern Transylvania to Hungary under the Second Vienna Award, and Southern Dobruja to Bulgaria under the Treaty of Craiova. Romania joined the Axis powers in 1940 and took part in the invasion of the Soviet Union, but following the Act of 23 August 1944 it switched sides to join the Allies. Romania regained Northern Transylvania in 1945, which the Paris Peace Treaties confirmed in 1947. Under Soviet occupation, King Michael I was forced to abdicate in December 1947, and Romania became a communist state, the Romanian People's Republic, and later a Warsaw Pact member. It was renamed the Socialist Republic of Romania in 1965. After the Romanian revolution of 1989 and the fall of communism, Romania began a transition to liberal democracy and a market economy.
Romania is a developed country with a high-income economy and one of the fastest growing economies in Europe, driven by a large industrial base,  with significant automotive manufacturing, pharmaceutical, mining, energy and weapons industries, as well as a major information technology industry, with major cities serving as regional technology centres. It is also known for its internet infrastructure, which ranks among the fastest in the world. Romania is regarded as a middle power in international relations and is a member of the European Union, NATO, and the BSEC, among other international organisations.

relations.title: China–Romania relations
relations.text:
The Kingdom of Romania and Republic of China (ROC) began relations on July 5, 1939.


== History ==
Following the takeover of the capital of Nanjing in 1941, Romania broke off relations with the ROC and began recognizing the Japanese-backed Chinese Republic. After the surrender of Japan, relations between the two never resumed, but after the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) seized power in 1949 and Romania abolished the monarchy in 1947, the Romanian People's Republic recognized People's Republic of China (PRC) as the legitimate government of China on October 5 of that year. China and Romania exchanged ambassadors for the first time in March 1950. 
When the Soviet Union and many other European communist countries withdrew their advisors from China in 1960, advisors from Yugoslavia were among those that remained. Relations between the Romania and China improved after Romania broke off ties with the Soviet Union in 1964.
On 27 December 1989, CCP General Secretary Jiang Zemin held a meeting of the Politburo Standing Committee regarding the situation in Romania, where the Romanian revolution led to the execution of Nicolae Ceaușescu. Despite long-standing ties with the previous government, China promptly recognized the new government.
China has an embassy in Bucharest and a consulate general in Constanța. Romania has an embassy in Beijing and 2 consulates general in Hong Kong and Shanghai. The modern-day Republic of China (Taiwan) has no official diplomatic relations with Romania, although it is represented by Hungary via the Hungarian Trade Office in Taipei and the ROC through the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Budapest.
In 2015, Romania signed an agreement with China General Nuclear Power Group for assistance in building civil nuclear power stations. When the National Liberal Party came into power, it cancelled all projects that the Social Democratic Party government had agreed to with China, including the nuclear power agreement, which Romania cancelled in 2020.


== Educational and cultural exchanges ==
Romania hosts four Confucius Institutes.


== Resident diplomatic missions ==
China has an embassy in Bucharest.
Romania has an embassy in Beijing and consulates-general in Hong Kong and Shanghai.

bri.title: Cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European Countries
bri.text: Cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European Countries (China-CEE, China-CEEC, also 14+1; formerly 17+1 from 2019 to 2021 and 16+1 from 2021 to 2022) is an initiative by the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs to promote business and investment relations between China and 14 countries of Central and Eastern Europe (CEE, CEEC): Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Greece, Hungary, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, and Slovenia. Prior to their 2022 withdrawal, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania were members of the initiative.

worldbank.title:
Livrabilul 6: Raport privind evaluarea ex-post a concursului național de
recrutare
worldbank.project: RO-Support to the National Agency for Civil Servants on Human Resource Management Reforms in Romania -- P503309
worldbank.abstract: În ultimul deceniu, România a urmărit un plan ambițios de modernizare a administrației sale publice, managementul resurselor umane (MRU) reprezentând o pârghie centrală pentru profesionalizare și guvernanță meritocratică. Ghidate de strategiile naționale de consolidare a administrației publice și de dezvoltare a funcției publice, reformele au urmărit să promoveze recrutarea transparentă și bazată pe merit, să îmbunătățească managementul performanței și să introducă parcursuri profesionale determinate de competențe. Obiectivul general a vizat trecerea de la practici de MRU fragmentate, bazate pe cunoștințe generale, la o arhitectură modernă și coerentă a RU, care să sprijine eficacitatea instituțională și servicii publice de calitate superioară.

worldbank.title: Utilizarea economică a  infrastructurii publice  de cercetare în România:  implicații privind  ajutorul de stat - Înregistrarea, monitorizarea și raportarea activității economice
worldbank.project: RO-Research modernization in Romania: improving the quality of and relevance of the research sector -- P179979
worldbank.abstract: Scopul acestui document este de a ghida beneficiarii fondurilor publice pentru RI în navigarea regulilor complexe privind ajutorul de stat. Scopul său este de a oferi un ghid pentru diverse cerințe legate de ajutorul de stat pentru beneficiarii finanțării UE pentru dezvoltarea și modernizarea RI. Ghidul arată cum beneficiarii pot explica și monitorizează utilizarea economică a RI finanțată public pentru a asigura respectarea regulilor UE privind ajutorul de stat. Aceasta explică faptul că beneficiarii trebuie să identifice entitatea relevantă pentru monitorizare (cum ar fi un laborator sau o facilitate), să aleagă și să aplice constant un parametru de capacitate (adesea de timp) care reflectă cel mai bine caracteristicile sale și să păstreze evidențe separate ale activități economice și non-economice folosind entitatea relevantă. Oferă șabloane pentru menținerea jurnalelor efective de utilizare pentru fiecare entitate relevantă și pentru întocmirea rapoartelor anuale, inclusiv situațiile financiare anuale care demonstrează separarea activităților, costurilor, finanțării și veniturilor. worldbank.title: Romania Poverty and Equity Brief : October 2026
worldbank.abstract: Romania has achieved one of the strongest improvements in living standards in the European Union since EU accession. Between 2015 and 2023, the country recorded the largest reduction in absolute poverty among EU member states and one of the strongest gains in shared prosperity. Poverty at the $8.3/day line (2021 PPP) fell from 30.9 percent to 5.1 percent, while anchored at-risk-of-poverty rates also declined sharply. Income growth became increasingly inclusive, with the bottom 40 percent experiencing faster income growth than the overall population, contributing to a marked decline in income inequality and a significant expansion of the middle class. Despite this remarkable progress and Romania’s transition to high-income status, key challenges remain. Romania continues to record among the highest levels of poverty and social exclusion in the EU, alongside pronounced urban-rural and regional disparities. The prosperity gap of 1.3 indicates that average incomes would still need to increase by about 30 percent to reach the global prosperity benchmark. Persistent inequalities in access to quality education, services, and economic opportunities continue to limit inclusive growth.

worldbank.title: Macro Poverty Outlook for Romania : Annual Meetings 2026
worldbank.abstract: Romania’s economy is projected to contract by an estimated 0.5 percent in 2026. Depressed private consumption is the main drag as real household incomes are squeezed by a renewed energy price shock compounding the 2025 electricity price cap removal and ongoing fiscal consolidation, amid restrained wage growth hitting poorer households hardest. A 2027 recovery hinges on political stability, a credible fiscal consolidation path, and sustained EU-funded investment.

worldbank.title:
Economic Use of Public Research Infrastructure in Romania: State Aid Implications - A Methodical Guidebook for Practitioners : Registering, Monitoring, and Reporting
on Economic Activity
worldbank.project: RO-Research modernization in Romania: improving the quality of and relevance of the research sector -- P179979
worldbank.abstract: The purpose of this document is to guide beneficiaries of public funds for RI in navigating the complex rules of State aid. It aims to provide a guide to various State aid–related requirements for beneficiaries of EU funding for the development and upgrading of RI. The guide shows how beneficiaries can account for and monitor the economic use of publicly funded RI to ensure compliance with EU State aid rules. It explains that beneficiaries must identify the relevant entity for monitoring (such as a lab or facility), choose and consistently apply a capacity parameter (often time) that best reflects its characteristics, and keep separate accounts of economic and non-economic activities using the relevant entity. It provides templates for maintaining actual usage logs for each relevant entity and for compiling annual reports, including annual financial statements that demonstrate the separation of activities, costs, funding, and revenues. It also includes a decision tree to classify activities and assess whether economic use remains purely ancillary or transitions to mixed use. Where monitoring identifies that State aid thresholds are exceeded, it explains how to apply the claw-back mechanism, including calculating the amount to be recovered by funding authorities, as set out in detailed examples. worldbank.title: Romanian Assistance for Post-Disaster Improvement and Development (RAPID) - Component 1: Country-specific technical assistance
worldbank.project: RO-Strengthening Disaster Risk Management Project -- P166302
worldbank.abstract: The objective of this project was to strengthen the capacity of civil protection institutions to ensure an effective and inclusive disaster response and recovery, and to improve existing recovery frameworks. The project combined technical analysis, institutional engagement, and knowledge sharing to support future efforts to strengthen the overarching framework and clarify roles and responsibilities during response and recovery, and in this way strengthen preparedness in Romania to future emergencies

worldbank.title: Decarbonizarea Sectorului Privat, Competitivitatea și Adaptarea la Schimbările Climatice în România : Analiza Programelor Care Sprijină Transformarea Ecologică a Sectorului Privat din Perspectiva Eficacității Politicilor
worldbank.project: RO-Supporting Romania's Green Industrial Plan and strengthening coordination for climate change initiatives (GRIN) -- P505862
worldbank.abstract: Tranziția verde la nivelul Uniunii Europene (UE) oferă noi oportunități de creștere a competitivității sectorului privat românesc, plasându-l pe o traiectorie de creștere durabilă din punct de vedere ecologic. Guvernul român s-a angajat să transforme obiectivele de decarbonizare în oportunități de creștere verde și a solicitat asistență Băncii Mondiale pentru a oferi contribuții la pregătirea unui Plan Industrial Verde. GRI RA utilizează un cadru analitic inovator care postulează că ecologizarea companiilor și creșterea rezilienței lor la schimbările climatice este crucială pentru competitivitatea sectorului privat pe termen lung și creșterea economică durabilă. Schimbările climatice generează diferite tipuri de riscuri pentru întreprinderi, dar pot crea și oportunități economice. Deoarece diverse bariere pot limita capacitatea firmelor de a gestiona riscurile și oportunitățile legate de climă, este necesară o acțiune a sectorului public pentru a se asigura că strategiile de atenuare și adaptare nu sunt doar adoptate, ci și concepute și implementate în moduri care sporesc oportunitățile economice. Activitățile care urmează să fie desfășurate de Banca Mondială în cadrul GRI RA sunt organizate în doi piloni. Primul pilon se concentrează pe sprijinirea dezvoltării și implementării Planului Industrial Verde, acoperind decarbonizarea industriei, adaptarea sectorului privat la schimbările climatice și competitivitatea verde. Al doilea pilon consolidează coordonarea instituțională,

worldbank.title: Artificial Intelligence in Romania’s Pre University Education
worldbank.abstract: This World Bank report presents a comprehensive analysis and strategic roadmap for integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) within Romania’s public pre-university education system. The primary objective of the study is to map the AI and EdTech landscape, assess the country’s readiness for AI adoption, and provide actionable recommendations to guide policymakers toward an equitable, coordinated, ethical, and sustainable use of AI technologies. The report examines AI applications supporting students, teachers, and school leaders, as well as the infrastructure, systemic, human-capacity, governance, and equity conditions affecting implementation. The study employed a multifaceted qualitative research approach. The methodology included semi-structured interviews between January and February 2026 with 21 stakeholders from government, the private sector, nongovernmental organizations, Romania’s AI Hub, and a rural school, complemented by platform documentation and secondary data on digital infrastructure, educational performance, digital skills, and EdTech adoption in Romania.

worldbank.title: Research Results Valuation Guidebook : A Guide for Romanian Public Research Organizations in Assigning an Economic Value to Early-stage Research Result
worldbank.project: RO-Research modernization in Romania: improving the quality of and relevance of the research sector -- P179979
worldbank.abstract: The purpose of this Guide is to equip Romanian PROs and their TTOs with a practical, internationally benchmarked framework for valuing and commercializing their early-stage research results. It focuses on the two primary IP commercialization pathways: licensing to established third parties and spinning out purpose-built companies. The framework is deliberately designed for institutions where commercialization expertise is still developing, prioritizing business awareness, clarity, and actionability over theoretical complexity.

worldbank.title: Building Resilience through Institutions, Communities & Knowledge : Proceedings from the 2026 BRICK Knowledge Exchange Event
worldbank.project: RO-Strengthening Disaster Risk Management Project -- P166302
worldbank.abstract: The BRICK 2026 Knowledge Exchange Event was organized as part of the Romanian Assistance for Post-Disaster Improvement and Development (RAPID) Project, financed under the Technical Assistance Financing Facility for Disaster Prevention and Preparedness (TAFF). The event took place in Bucharest from 24 to 27 March 2026, bringing together more than 100 practitioners and experts from across Europe and Asia to share lessons on disaster recovery, emergency preparedness and response, and how to put the right “bricks” in place for more resilient societies. Designed around the concept of ‘Building Resilience through Institutions, Communities and Knowledge’, the event offered a platform for peer-to-peer learning, drawing lessons for current and future recovery efforts and showcasing knowledge developed through activities implemented through TAFF.

worldbank.title: From Ambition to Impact : Closing the AI Readiness Gap in Europe and Central Asia's Education Systems - Findings and Policy Priorities from Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye
worldbank.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering Europe and Central Asia's classrooms faster than education systems can govern its use. This note synthesizes the AI Readiness Assessment applied in Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye, a rapid mixed-methods diagnostic of governance, infrastructure, teacher capacity, and equity. The three countries show convergent ambition, divergent pathways, and a persistent gap between national strategy and classroom practice. Four bottlenecks recur: an adoption ceiling in digital and higher-order skills; governance and financing frictions; weak public-private coordination; and an evidence deficit, with no institutionalized demand for evaluating effects on learning. Scaling therefore depends less on technological readiness than on evidence quality and system coherence, which shape the micro and macro priorities set out here.

openalex.title: China’s ‘One Belt, One Road’ Plan and Romania
openalex.abstract: 2015년 4월, 마르마라 그룹 재단(Marmara Group Foundation)이 주최한 18 번째 유라시아 경제정상회담(Eurasian Economic Summit)에 참석한 에밀 콘스탄티네스쿠(Emil Constantinescu) 전 루마니아 대통령은 “실크로드 프로젝 트의 부활은 1990년대에 시작되었을 때에는 유토피아였을지 모르지만, 오늘날에는 그 꿈이 점차 현실화되고 있다”고 언급하였다. 역사적으로 볼 때, 루마니아는 동서는 물론 남북의 교차로에 위치하고 있어 전략적으로 중요한 요충지였다. 흑해 역시 그동안 동양과 서양의 중요한 연결고리 역할을 하였으며, 특히 오늘날 흑해 최대의 항구이자 유럽에서 4대 항구인 콘스탄차(Constanţa)는 ‘일대일로’ 사업과 관련하여 중요한 거점 항구로 간주되고 있다. 따라서 루마니아 정부는 유라시아의 다른 나라들처럼 중국의 ‘일대일로’ 사업에 커다란 관심을 가지고 있다. 하지만 최근 들어 중국 시진핑 지도부가 야심차게 추진해 온 ‘일대일로’ 사업이 차질을 빚고 있다. 즉 최근 일대일로 사업 참여국들이 빚더미에 올라앉으면서 반중정서를 드러내고 있는데, 파키스탄과 스리랑카, 네팔, 미얀마 그리고 말레이시아 등과 같은 국가들은 일대일로 사업을 전면 재검토에 들어갔거나 중국과의 협력을 폐기하려하고 있다. 특히 파키스탄은 ‘일대일로 사업’을 위해 중국으로부터 차관을 들였지만 고율의 이자와 사업의 비경제성 때문에 IMF 에 구제금융을 신청할 위기에 처해있다. 따라서 이들 국가들은 상대적으로 이자율이 낮은 IMF로부터 구제금융을 받길 원하고 있지만 얼마 전 트럼프미 대통령은 ‘뉴 실크로드’ 참여국에게 금융지원을 하지 않겠다고 단호하게 밝혔다. 일대일로 사업에 참여한 동남아시아 국가들이 유동성 악화를 겪고 있는 이유는 여러 가지가 있겠지만 그 중에서 가장 큰 요인은 중국이 이들 국가들에게 차관을 제공하는 것에 끝나지 않고 중국 기업이 사업 시공업체로 선정되게끔 정치·경제적으로 영향력을 행사하고 있기 때문이다. 즉 그동안 동남아 국가들은 중국으로부터 차관을 들여와 사업을 시작하였지만 공사를 맡은 중국 기업이 고스란히 공사대금을 가져감으로써 이들 국가에게는 거액의 빚만 남게 되었다. 상황이 이러하면 중국공산당도 이들 국가들을 경제적으로 지원을 할 수도 있겠지만 오히려 원금과 이자를 제대로 갚지 못하는 나라들의 항구를 빼앗아 버렸는데, 대표적인 곳이 스리랑카의 함반 토타(Hambantota)항이다. 물론 이를 지켜본 다른 국가들은 중국으로부터 거액의 차관을 도입했다가 스리랑카처럼 자국의 영토를 빼앗기지 않을까 우려하고 있다. 따라서 최근들어 궁지에 몰린 이들 국가들은 아예 ‘일대일로 사업’에서 탈퇴하려는 움직임을 보이고 있다. 외환위기 직전까지 몰린 파키 스탄과 네팔은 자국의 일대일로 관련 사업을 중단한다고 밝혔으며 말레이 시아도 동부해안철도(ECRL)와 고속철 사업을 전격 취소한다고 밝혔다. 특히 미얀마는 90억 달러 규모의 차우크퓨 항만 공사를 취소한다고 밝혔는데, 이것은 중국에게는 큰 타격이 되었다. 유럽에서도 상황은 비슷하다고 볼 수 있다. 2018년 2월, 앙겔라 메르켈 (Angela Merkel) 독일 총리는 중국이 서부 발칸반도에 대한 투자를 미끼로 정치적 목적을 달성하려 해서는 안 된다고 경고하기 시작하였다. 이처럼 영국에 이어 프랑스, 독일 등도 ‘일대일로 사업’에 부정적인 견해를 보이고 있다. 하지만 중국의 입장에서 가장 곤혹스러운 것은 날로 격화되고 있는 미국과의 갈등이다. 오늘날 유럽과 아시아에서의 영향력 확대를 꿈꾸던 중국 공산당의 꿈은 점점 더 멀어져가는 것처럼 보인다.The Silk Road was an ancient network of trade routes, formally established during the Han Dynasty of China. openalex.title: Could Romania Become a Trade Hub on the TEN-T and the Belt and Road Initiative?
openalex.abstract: - In the context of the current trade wars, the major players are aiming at identifying new opportunities to keep the multilateral trade engine running. With the Belt and Road, a modern version of the ancient Silk Road, China launched an initiative that could encompass many stakeholders from various continents aiming to place herself at the core of the new world order.This research focuses on the main transportation corridors of the Belt and Road initiative, analysing them through the lenses of several relevant indicators, to identify their attractiveness degree for the EU and China and thus answering the question in the title.The analysis is based mainly on data provided by the World Bank, Eurostat, the National Bureau of Statistics of China

openalex.title: The importance of Chinese investments in the One Belt, One Road Initiative
openalex.abstract:
The 16+1 cooperation initiative, involving the People’s Republic
of China and the 16 countries of Central and Eastern Europe, was officially
launched in 2012. Each of the countries has its own cooperation priorities,
but the majority of the investment projects which are part of the initiative
is in the areas of transport infrastructure, agriculture, energy, logistics,
health, etc. This cooperation initiative is complementary to China’s
landmark foreign policy project, One Belt, One Road; together, they
determine China’s attitude towards these 16 countries. Firstly, this paper
will view the main sectors of Chinese investment throughout the countries
of Central and Eastern Europe since 2012. This will be followed by the
investment projects which have been completed, as well as the most recent
announced projects and their estimated value. Five years after the official
launching of the 16+1 cooperation initiative, it is clear that not all countries
in the region have benefited equally from the initiative ‐ while some have
maintained enthusiasm due to a large number of implemented projects
and tangible results, the others are still waiting to see tax revenue flowing
into their budgets and are growing sceptical. The authors point out that
dominant countries such as Hungary, Poland, the Czech Republic, Romania,
Serbia or Bulgaria have seen most of the benefits; although it is unrealistic
to expect equal benefits to all 16 countries of Central and Eastern Europe,
the initiative will be fully successful only if major Chinese companies gain
a stronghold in those countries in which they were absent until now.

openalex.title: Belt and Road Initiative and Possible Implications for Central and Eastern Europe Countries
openalex.abstract: - Many of the Central and Eastern Europe Countries (CEEC) that are subject to The “16+1” Platform under China’s Belt and Road Initiative, including Romania, are member states of the European Union (EU) and their economic development strategies are implicitly dependent on the European Union’s goals, financing mechanisms and regulations. On the other hand, the CEEC’s geographical position, bridging Asia and Western Europe and their economic potential in the global value and production chain make them indispensable for BRI integration within Eurasia. Furthermore, in a more and more restrictive European context, due to Brexit and the refugee crisis, meeting the financing needs for development and economic growth is crucial for this group of countries in order to ensure their real convergence with the more developed West.In such a context, the present paper aims at bringing a contribution to the following pressing question for Brussels, in terms of geopolitical and economic concerns, namely, whether BRI can become a complementary support instrument to the European policies fostering CEEC’s integration with the West and not a competitive strategy hindering EU’s interests. To this aim, we try to investigate some of the features of specific cases of similar infrastructure investments in CEEC, financed by European funds and within the BRI framework, respectively, in order to have a base for a comparative analysis.

openalex.title: Central and Eastern European countries between the 16+1 platform and Chinese OBOR - One Belt, One Road - Initiative
openalex.abstract: This paper aims at analysing the projects and the initiatives of the Central and Eastern European countries that have been finalised, are in progress or will be developed in the near future with the help of the existing or future financial instruments specific to the 16+1 platform and the One Belt, One Road complex program. For our research we selected four countries, namely: Poland, Romania, Serbia and Hungary, the group being relevant from the perspective of the transportation corridors connected to the ”One Belt, One Road” initiative: (1) - Piraeus, Skopje, Belgrade, Budapest, Western Europe; (2) - Suez Canal, Constanta and then Danube, Western Europe, or through Moldova towards Ukraine and Poland; (3) – Constanta, through the Black Sea and Caspian Sea and then the corridors mentioned at the previous point. We based our analysis on the data provided by the National Bureau of Statistics of China, China-CEEC think-tank network and the literature in the field.

openalex.title: CHINESE ENGAGEMENT IN LATIN AMERICA AND EUROPE: INSIGHTS FOR ROMANIA
openalex.venue: Proceedings of the ... International Scientific Conference "Strategies XXI". Romania in the New International Security Dynamics/Proceedings of the ... International Scientific Conference "Strategies XXI". Romania and the New Dynamics of the International Security
openalex.abstract: This paper examines Chinese commercial, political, and security engagement with Latin America and the Caribbean, comparing it with similar engagement in Europe. It findsevidence that PRC engagement globally is driven by a strategy focused on re-orienting the world to the economic benefit of the PRC, with nonetheless important political, institutional,and security engagement in support of these objectives and the consequences of their pursuit. It finds common elements in China’s pursuit of secure sources of supply, markets andtechnology across regions, its use of the PRC government supporting roles, with differences reflecting the governance and political structure of each partner, the economic opportunitiesavailable, and the imperatives of geography. It finds that PRC “soft power” over political and business elites in both regions is significant, based more in the expectation of benefit than analignment of values, and thus can coexist with mistrust of the PRC. It finds that Europe can not only gain insights from examining Chinese engagement in Latin America, but that engagementimpacts Europe directly through the roles of its companies as both competitors and partners of European ones in the region, and through intraregional supply chains and the flows of fundsthrough mergers and acquisitions by China of stakes in European companies.Keywords: PRC, China, Latin America, Belt and Road, BRI, Infrastructure, Security Engagement.

openalex.title: Evaluating economic, geographic, and strategic drivers of China's renewable energy Investments: Insights from BRI and institutional
openalex.abstract: This study assesses the viability of China's renewable energy investments in the middle corridor of the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), with an eye toward six Black Sea coastal nations—Romania, Turkey, Bulgaria, Ukraine, Georgia, and Russia. Using national and international data including the Global Governance Indicators, IRENA, UN Comtrade, and China's overseas investment records—this study employs a hybrid Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) methodology. It combines the Adaptive Evaluating Technique based on Adaptive Standardized Intervals (ARTASI) for evaluating investment locations and the Spherical Fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process (SF-AHP) for weighting multidimensional risk variables. Guiding international cooperation theory, the model combines geopolitical, institutional, environmental, and financial concerns. Supported by great institutional capacity, strategic alignment, and economic infrastructure, results show Romania and Turkey as the most appealing places for Chinese renewable energy investments. The sensitivity study supports the model's resilience over several weighting situations. The study offers legislators practical information emphasizing the need for strategic alignment, diplomatic cooperation, and institutional preparation in cross-border renewable energy projects. It advises BRI players to build diplomatic and legal systems to lower uncertainty and enhance investment results in areas of political sensitivity.

openalex.title: Introduction
openalex.abstract: This introduction presents an overview of the key concepts covered in the subsequent chapters of this book. The book introduces the background to and main trends of Chinese foreign policy, with special reference to China and Central and Eastern Europe (CEE) relations. It addresses China's bilateral relations with specific countries in CEE, including the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania and the Balkan states. The book then sets the broad context of current China's domestic politics and foreign policy under President Xi Jinping. It also provides a detailed account of how China has developed relations with Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs) over the past two decades, with a particular focus on the 16 + 1 process and the One Belt, One Road (OBOR) initiative. The book analyzes the characteristics of China's economic relations with CEECs, with a focus on China's investment and trade flows to the region and the underlying motivations for them.
